credit: Contributed by volunteer annotators, recorded under the pseudonyms they chose. Proposed upstream to OpenCRE with credit.
description: Human-curated traditional-control -> AI-hub links, closing the structural gap that the AI and traditional CRE hub regions are disjoint: 78 AI hubs and 380 traditional hubs with an intersection of exactly 0, so nothing in the curated gold positions a traditional control against an AI hub.
limits: The candidate hub sheet was derived from BRIDGE_AI_FRAMEWORK_IDS, which includes the frameworks supplying Gate 2's evaluation gold. The support set therefore could not have missed the gold, and any downstream result licenses a claim about this hub region rather than about bridging in general. Checkpoint-2 item C6, disclosed and not fixed.

The round-1 handbook stated the answer distribution before annotators had read anything. Round 2 removed that sentence and re-ran the same 300 controls with the same two people: 106 NONE->link, 0 reversals, 0 hub changes. Neither round's link rate is established as a property of the task, and docs/phase2c-results.md section 4 governs what may be reported.

Inter-annotator agreement depends on the denominator. On the link/no-link decision Cohen's kappa is 0.597 (round 1) and 0.508 (round 2); on WHICH hub, among controls both annotators linked, it is 0.885 and 0.891. Quote the denominator with the figure.
Contributors retain a right to withdraw. `scripts/build_gate2_corpus.py --exclude-annotator` re-cuts the corpus; a model already trained on it cannot be un-trained.

links.rationale: Terminating logical sessions when access conditions expire supports inference access control, although the control is not limited to inference sessions.
Defining which actions may occur without authentication sets the access boundary for a service, including an inference service.
links.section_name: AC-14 Permitted Actions Without Identification or Authentication

links.rationale: Authorizing accounts and removing obsolete access directly supports access control to inference, although the control governs system accounts more broadly.
Reviewing proposed public content and removing nonpublic information shares the disclosure prevention purpose of sensitive AI output handling, although publication governance is broader.

AC-23 protects data stores from unauthorized extraction through query patterns, and its listed techniques (limiting query number and frequency, limiting response detail, differential privacy, flagging atypical queries) are exactly the defenses against extracting training data from a model through inference; the model is the data store and inference is the query.
Applying an authorization decision to each service access request directly matches controlling access to AI inference.
A reference monitor enforces authorization on every resource access and can implement inference access control, although the specified mechanism is broader.
Enforcing approved authorizations for application and service resources has the same purpose as enforcing access control to AI inference.
Restricting users and processes to the privileges necessary for assigned tasks directly matches minimization of model action privileges.
Limiting failed authentication attempts protects access to an inference service, although it concerns logon attempts rather than model input attacks.
Maintaining security awareness and training policies supports governance of AI security education, although the training subject is not restricted to AI.
Providing and updating security literacy and awareness education matches the educational purpose of the AI security education hub.
Providing security training tailored to personnel responsibilities directly matches the purpose of AI security education.
Documenting and monitoring personnel training supports administration of AI security education, although records alone do not deliver that education.
Providing feedback on security training results supports evaluation and improvement of AI security education.
Generating records of selected security events directly supports observation of inference activity, although the control applies to any system component.
Capturing the content of user sessions supports observation of inference interactions, although the control also covers unrelated session activity.
Selecting security relevant events and query parameters to log supports monitoring inference activity, although the event scope is system wide.
Recording event type, source, outcome, and actor supplies the observation details needed for inference monitoring, although it defines general audit content.
Analyzing activity records for unusual or inappropriate use matches inference monitoring when the observed activity is inference.
links.section_name: AU-6 Audit Record Review, Analysis, and Reporting

links.rationale: Reducing audit records into analyzable reports supports inference monitoring, although the control also covers general incident investigation.
links.section_name: AU-7 Audit Record Reduction and Report Generation

links.rationale: Assessing whether security controls operate correctly and produce their intended outcomes matches AI security assurance, although the assessment is not AI specific.
Assigning officials to accept operational risk and authorize systems supports AI management accountability, although it does not define the complete management system.
Repeatedly assessing control effectiveness provides continuing security assurance rather than merely observing inference traffic.

Continuous monitoring keeps ongoing awareness of security state by monitoring defined metrics at defined frequencies, and AI model performance validation does that for the model by repeatedly testing its behaviour so that drift or a poisoning attack shows up as a change; the argument against is that CA-7's metrics measure control effectiveness rather than model behaviour, and Monitor inference (703-813) is another plausible home.
Testing whether adversaries can exploit system weaknesses matches the verification purpose of AI security assurance and validation.
Controlling software use against license and copyright obligations supports AI compliance management, although the control addresses software generally.
Verifying approved digital signatures before component installation supports model supply chain authenticity, although the control also covers nonmodel software and firmware.
Maintaining an approved baseline under configuration control supports integrity of a deployed model's configuration, although the baseline also covers other system components.
Approving, recording, and monitoring changes prevents unauthorized alteration of deployed components and therefore supports runtime model integrity.
Restricting who can change a deployed component directly protects its integrity, including when that component is a runtime model.
Restricting a system to mission essential capabilities matches limiting the actions available to a model, although functionality reduction is broader than privilege reduction.
Requiring stronger authentication under suspicious access conditions reinforces inference access control rather than analyzing the semantic content of model inputs.
Requiring users to authenticate again when access circumstances change supports continued authorization to use an inference service.
Issuing identity assertions and access tokens for authorization decisions directly supports access control to inference, although the identity infrastructure serves other resources too.
links.section_name: IA-13 Identity Providers and Authorization Servers

links.rationale: Authenticating organizational users and their processes supplies identity assurance for inference access control, although the control applies to all system access.
Maintaining strong authenticators and revoking compromised credentials protects authenticated inference access, although the credential scope is broader.
Authenticating external users and their processes supports controlled access to inference services, although it also applies to other services.
Authenticating services and applications before communication supports trusted participants in inference access, although the control is not limited to inference.
Training users and responders to recognize and handle security incidents shares the purpose of AI security education, although incident coverage is general.
Documenting system context, responsibilities, risks, and planned controls supports structured AI management, although the control covers security and privacy planning more generally.
links.section_name: PL-2 System Security and Privacy Plans

links.rationale: Centrally planning, implementing, assessing, and monitoring controls matches coordinated AI management, although the centrally managed controls are not limited to AI.
Establishing an organization wide security program with responsibilities, management commitment, controls, and review matches the management system purpose in an AI context.
Integrating authorization responsibilities and ongoing risk acceptance into organizational governance matches a management system function for AI.
Developing security workforce knowledge, skills, qualifications, and role training supports AI security education, although the workforce scope is broader.
Coordinating execution of organizational testing, training, and monitoring plans supports management system operation rather than one specific AI test.
Maintaining professional contacts to support continuing security education and current practices fits AI security education, although information sharing is also a purpose.
links.section_name: PM-15 Security and Privacy Groups and Associations

links.rationale: Translating mandatory information protection requirements into policy for external systems supports compliance management, although AI is only one possible system context.
links.section_name: PM-17 Protecting Controlled Unclassified Information on External Systems

links.rationale: Establishing privacy objectives, accountability, resources, controls, and review supplies a privacy governance component of an AI management system.
Appointing an accountable privacy leader supports allocation of governance responsibilities within an AI management system.
Appointing an accountable leader to coordinate and maintain the security program provides the leadership function of an AI management system.
links.section_name: PM-2 Information Security Program Leadership Role

links.rationale: Establishing review and correction processes for inaccurate or outdated personal information shares the purpose of data quality control.
links.section_name: PM-22 Personally Identifiable Information Quality Management

links.rationale: Minimizing personal information used in testing, training, and research directly implements the data minimization purpose.
links.section_name: PM-25 Minimization of Personally Identifiable Information Used in Testing, Training, and Research

links.rationale: Reporting to demonstrate accountability against statutory, regulatory, and policy requirements matches compliance management in an AI privacy context.
Establishing risk assumptions, constraints, priorities, and tolerance supports the governance basis of an AI management system.
Assigning senior accountability and a coordinated risk executive function supports organizational AI management responsibilities.
links.section_name: PM-29 Risk Management Program Leadership Roles

links.rationale: Allocating and making resources available for security and privacy programs supports operation of an AI management system, although the budgeting obligation is broader.
links.section_name: PM-3 Information Security and Privacy Resources

links.rationale: Establishing and reviewing a strategy to manage supplier risks across the system life cycle matches AI supply chain management at the broader system level.
links.section_name: PM-30 Supply Chain Risk Management Strategy

links.rationale: Governing organizational monitoring metrics, assessments, responses, and reporting supports continuing evaluation of an AI management system.
Reviewing whether systems remain within their intended mission supports oversight of AI use within an AI management system, although the control is technology neutral.
Coordinating and prioritizing remediation across organizational risk programs supports management system improvement rather than a specific model protection.
links.section_name: PM-4 Plan of Action and Milestones Process

links.rationale: Measuring security program and control effectiveness supports evaluation of an AI management system rather than validation of model predictive performance.
Defining and consistently applying risk tolerance, assessment methods, mitigation strategies, and monitoring supports the risk governance of an AI management system.
Disabling access and revoking credentials on termination directly removes authorization to use inference services, although the control also covers property and exit interviews.
Revising access authorizations after personnel transfers supports continued control over who may use inference services.
Requiring and monitoring personnel security conditions for external technology providers supports AI supply chain management, although the control is limited to supplier workforce risks.
Assigning security and privacy responsibilities in position descriptions supports accountability within an AI management system, although roles are not AI specific.
Determining the authority for personal information processing and restricting processing to authorized activities supports AI compliance management.
links.section_name: PT-2 Authority to Process Personally Identifiable Information

links.rationale: Documenting permitted processing purposes and controlling incompatible changes supports compliance management, rather than reducing the amount of data collected.
links.section_name: PT-3 Personally Identifiable Information Processing Purposes

links.rationale: Explaining personal information processing clearly to interacting individuals shares the transparency purpose for AI users, although the notice is not specific to model behavior.
Preparing, publishing, and maintaining required system notices implements a privacy compliance obligation that can apply to an AI system.
Independently verifying matching results and allowing people to contest adverse decisions shares human oversight's purpose, although record matching need not use AI.

Risk assessment identifies threats, vulnerabilities, likelihood and impact, and an AI management system is built around exactly that assessment for AI systems; rated 2 because the hub is the governance system as a whole and RA-3 is one process within it.
Scanning and analyzing applications for exploitable weaknesses contributes to AI security assurance, although the control also covers conventional infrastructure vulnerabilities.
Choosing whether to mitigate, accept, transfer, or avoid identified risk implements risk decision making within an AI management system.
Assessing personal data handling for conformity to privacy requirements supports AI compliance management, although privacy risk assessment extends beyond compliance.

A privacy impact assessment analyzes how personal information will be processed before technology is built or bought, and an impact assessment of that kind is a core process of an AI management system that takes responsibility for AI risk to individuals; the argument against is that RA-8 is privacy-specific and the hub is framed around AI security.
Maintaining policies and procedures for secure system acquisition supports AI supply chain management, although the acquisition scope is broader.
Requiring developers to test security controls, document results, and correct discovered flaws directly matches the development verification purpose of AI security assurance.
Requiring documented development processes and protecting their tools and changes supports AI supply chain integrity, although it also applies to development unrelated to AI.
links.section_name: SA-15 Development Process, Standards, and Tools

links.rationale: Teaching personnel to operate security and privacy controls correctly directly matches the purpose of AI security education.
Allocating explicit budgets to security and privacy requirements supports implementation of AI management, although the control addresses an individual system or service.
Requiring external developers to satisfy trust and personnel screening criteria addresses supplier workforce risk within AI supply chain management.
Replacing unsupported components or arranging alternate supplier support addresses life cycle supply chain risk, although the component scope is broader than AI.
Integrating responsibilities and security risk management throughout the system life cycle supports coordinated AI management rather than any one model training technique.
Putting security requirements, supplier responsibilities, and acceptance criteria into acquisition contracts directly supports AI supply chain management.
Requiring and monitoring security controls from external service providers matches oversight of model hosting suppliers, although other outsourced services are also covered.
Preventing session hijacking and false information insertion supports integrity of runtime model exchanges, although the control is not confined to AI sessions.
Protecting stored system artifacts from unauthorized disclosure matches runtime model confidentiality when the stored artifact is the deployed model.
links.section_name: SC-28 Protection of Information at Rest

links.rationale: Heterogeneity uses diverse technologies so that compromising one does not compromise everything, protecting against common-mode failure including supply chain attacks, and Ensemble AI models does the same by combining models trained on separate data so that poisoning one source has limited effect; the argument against is that SC-29 is about diversity of platforms while the hub is about diversity of models and training sets.
Executing protected component images from immutable media supports runtime model integrity when the deployed model is part of that image.
Restricting disclosure of design specifications, testing protocols, and security implementation details directly supports protection of technical AI information.
Separating execution domains and constraining untrusted processes limits access to other resources, matching model action privilege minimization when the process executes model actions.
Preventing residual data from passing between users supports model input confidentiality when shared inference resources retain prior users' inputs.
links.section_name: SC-4 Information in Shared System Resources

links.rationale: Preventing or limiting service denial addresses the availability objective of AI resource exhaustion protection, although the control also covers other denial mechanisms.
Allocating resources by quotas and priorities directly matches limiting inference resources to preserve availability.
Protecting transmitted information against modification shares the purpose of runtime model input and output integrity, although the control also permits a confidentiality focus.
Rejecting inputs with invalid syntax, ranges, or content matches anomalous AI input handling, although conventional validation does not cover all semantic AI attacks.

Input validation prescreens inputs so that malformed or hostile content is rejected before it reaches the application, which is the same purpose as validating and sanitizing prompts before they reach a model; rated 2 because SI-10 is about syntax, format and range checks while prompt defenses work on natural language, and Anomalous AI input handling (342-641) is another plausible home for the semantic side of the control.
Preventing error messages from revealing stack traces and implementation details supports protection of technical AI information, although the control also covers other sensitive information.
Applying legal and operational retention requirements across the information life cycle matches training data retention management when the retained information is training data.

Output filtering validates program output and blocks unexpected content before it is displayed, and Sensitive AI output handling filters model output for content that should not reach the user; the alternative reading is Encode model output (430-722), which handles injection into downstream systems.
Automatically validating and suppressing unexpected application outputs matches oversight that limits unwanted model behavior, although the control does not specify AI outputs.
Checking and correcting data accuracy, relevance, timeliness, and completeness directly matches the data quality control purpose.
links.section_name: SI-18 Personally Identifiable Information Quality Operations

links.rationale: De-identification removes identifying elements from datasets, and Training data obfuscation applies that same anonymization or pseudonymization to data before it is used for training.

Tainting embeds markers in data or components so the organization can tell when they have been exfiltrated, and Watermarking AI models embeds a mark so a stolen or copied model can be recognized; rated 2 because the hub may also cover output watermarking, which has a different purpose.
Deleting information when it is no longer needed and minimizing its retention period matches training data retention management for training datasets.

System monitoring detects attacks, indicators of attack and unauthorized use through strategically placed monitoring, and Monitor inference is that monitoring placed at the model's inference interface.
Verifying that security and privacy functions operate correctly provides security assurance, although the tested functions need not be AI specific.
links.section_name: SI-6 Security and Privacy Function Verification

links.rationale: Security function verification periodically checks that a function still operates correctly and alerts or halts on failure, and validating that a deployed model still performs as expected is that check applied to the model; the argument against is that the hub sits under development-time verification.
links.section_name: SI-6 Security and Privacy Function Verification

links.rationale: Detecting and responding to unauthorized changes in hosted software and information directly matches integrity verification for a runtime model.
links.section_name: SI-7 Software, Firmware, and Information Integrity

links.rationale: Maintaining supply chain risk policies, responsibilities, and procedures directly supports AI supply chain management, although the covered supply chains are broader.
Inspecting externally handled components for tampering supports AI model supply chain integrity, although the control also covers physical equipment.
links.section_name: SR-10 Inspection of Systems or Components

links.rationale: Detecting and preventing counterfeit components before entry into a system matches authenticity control within an AI model supply chain.
Securely disposing of supplied components and preventing their entry into the gray market addresses the disposal stage of AI supply chain management.
Planning and reviewing supplier risk controls across acquisition, operation, and disposal matches life cycle AI supply chain management.
links.section_name: SR-2 Supply Chain Risk Management Plan

links.rationale: Supply chain controls and processes identify and address weaknesses in supply chain elements and apply controls against supply chain risk, which is what AI supply chain management does for data, models and hosting.
links.section_name: SR-3 Supply Chain Controls and Processes

links.rationale: Provenance documents and maintains the origin, ownership, location and change history of systems, components and associated data, and provenance of models and training data is central to AI supply chain management; I chose the parent hub because the control spans both the data (423-055) and model (852-770) children.
Using acquisition strategies, procurement controls, and contract requirements to reduce supplier threats directly supports AI supply chain management.
links.section_name: SR-5 Acquisition Strategies, Tools, and Methods

links.rationale: Assessing suppliers and their subordinate providers for security and supply chain risks matches supplier evaluation within AI supply chain management.
Protecting supply chain design specifications, configurations, security requirements, and test results supports confidentiality of technical AI information.
Establishing supplier notification agreements for compromises and assessment results supports risk coordination across an AI supply chain.
Preventing modification and substitution of components supports runtime model integrity, although the program also covers distribution and reverse engineering.

A tamper protection program guards components against modification and substitution during distribution and in use, and verifying that a sourced model arrived unaltered is part of AI model supply chain management; Runtime model integrity controls (276-748) is the alternative reading for the in-use half.

name: TRACT Phase 2C bridge corpus
provenance: Tier 2 under results/phase1b/CAMPAIGN3.md section 2: independently human-authored, with no model output shown to the annotator at any point. Two annotators independently judged 300 NIST SP 800-53 controls against a sheet of 78 AI-region CRE hubs carrying only hub id, name, hierarchy path and branch. Weaker than Tier 1, which asserts OpenCRE curated it independently of TRACT; far stronger than Tier 3, which is produced by or ratified in the presence of a model.
